endorsements.quote: In hospitals with limited data infrastructure, local validation may begin pragmatically through small-scale silent testing, clinician review of outputs, comparison with observed outcomes, documentation of false alerts and missed events, and staged use before full clinical integration.

In hospitals with limited data infrastructure, local validation may begin pragmatically through small-scale silent testing, clinician review of outputs, comparison with observed outcomes, documentation of false alerts and missed events, and staged use before full clinical integration.

Local validation before deployment is essential because models developed in better resourced or different populations may perform poorly when case mix, documentation practices, monitoring frequency, laboratory access, or postoperative follow-up differ.

For perioperative services, this means that AI tools should be introduced with clearly defined clinical scope, human oversight, documentation of performance, processes for override and escalation, attention to data stewardship, and mechanisms for post-implementation review.

For perioperative services, this means that AI tools should be introduced with clearly defined clinical scope, human oversight, documentation of performance, processes for override and escalation, attention to data stewardship, and mechanisms for post-implementation review.

Tools should be locally validated, clinically supervised, and judged not only by algorithmic performance but also by their effect on postoperative complications, recovery, cost, workflow, staff trust, and equity.
Procurement decisions should require evidence of clinical scope, data requirements, human oversight, cybersecurity safeguards, bias assessment, local validation plans, and post deployment monitoring.
Hospitals should avoid purchasing isolated digital tools that are not connected to ERAS pathways, escalation protocols, staff training, patient safety metrics, and accountability structures.

Workforce digital literacy is a key determinant because clinicians, nurses, anaesthesia providers, data officers, and managers must understand what digital tools can and cannot do, how alerts should be interpreted, how data quality affects outputs, and when human escalation is required.
These tools may strengthen efficiency and situational awareness, but they should not be mistaken for substitutes for clinical judgment or for the foundational requirements of safe perioperative care.

unlisted_practices: Establish essential perioperative safety infrastructure (monitoring, oxygen, checklists, recovery observation) before deploying AI in resource-limited settings.
Implement context-adapted ERAS pathways to generate baseline data before adopting AI.
Consider AI model development only when data quality, governance, representativeness, and validation capacity are adequate.
Conduct regular multidisciplinary review of adherence, outcomes, alert performance, staff concerns, and unintended consequences, with protocol refinement.
Govern AI implementation as a quality improvement and implementation research agenda rather than a technology purchase.
Limit early AI use in resource-limited settings to bounded, supportive rather than autonomous applications.
